records.question: How do I start going to the gym?
alternative_phrasings: What should my first workout be?
records.short_answer: Start with two or three manageable full-body sessions per week and learn a few basic movement patterns.
records.detailed_explanation: A simple plan is easier to repeat and progress. Start with stable exercises, moderate effort and enough rest. Technique and consistency matter more than complicated splits.
records.practical_recommendation: Choose 5–7 movements covering squat, hinge, push, pull and trunk; use 1–3 sets and stop with several good reps left initially.
records.misconception: You need a six-day split or advanced supplements to make progress.
records.warning: Stop and seek professional advice for red-flag symptoms or relevant medical restrictions.

records.question: How many days per week should I train?
records.short_answer: Choose the number of days you can attend consistently and recover from; two or more resistance sessions per week is a useful general starting point.
records.detailed_explanation: Frequency distributes weekly work and practice. The best split is the one that fits the goal, schedule and recovery, not the one with the most days.
records.practical_recommendation: Start with 2–3 days for beginners; use 3–4 for many intermediate plans; add days only when there is a reason.
records.misconception: More gym days automatically means more muscle.
records.warning: Do not train through illness, unusual pain or significant fatigue.
records.evidence_text: High for general activity; exact split individualised

records.question: What is progressive overload?
alternative_phrasings: How do I get stronger over time?
Do I add weight every week?
records.short_answer: Progressive overload means gradually increasing the challenge your body can handle while maintaining good technique.
records.detailed_explanation: You can progress reps, load, sets, range, control or exercise difficulty. It does not mean adding weight every session regardless of readiness.
records.practical_recommendation: Use a rep range; when all sets reach the top with target effort and technique, add a small amount of load.
records.misconception: You must add weight every workout.
records.warning: If pain or technique breakdown appears, stop the progression and reassess.
records.evidence_text: High principle; exact method coaching application

records.question: How many sets and reps should I do?
records.short_answer: There is no single best rep range for everyone; choose sets and reps based on goal, exercise, effort and experience.
records.detailed_explanation: Strength benefits from practising heavier loads; hypertrophy can occur across a broad range when sets are sufficiently challenging and weekly volume is appropriate.
records.practical_recommendation: Begin with 2–3 work sets per exercise; use moderate reps for many exercises and adjust based on goal and comfort.
records.misconception: 10 reps is the only muscle-building range.
records.warning: Avoid maximal effort testing without appropriate experience and supervision.

records.question: Do I need to train to failure?
alternative_phrasings: Should every set be to failure?
records.short_answer: No. Training to failure is not required for every set or every exercise.
records.detailed_explanation: Stopping with a few good reps left can produce productive training while managing fatigue. Failure may be used selectively on safer exercises.
records.practical_recommendation: Most sets can finish around 1–3 RIR; use more reserve on new or technical movements.
records.misconception: If a set does not end in failure it was wasted.
records.warning: Do not take heavy technical lifts to failure without suitable safeguards.
records.evidence_text: High that failure is not universally required

records.question: What does RIR mean?
records.short_answer: RIR means how many additional good-quality repetitions you think you could complete before failure.
records.detailed_explanation: 2 RIR means you stop when you estimate two more clean reps were possible. It is a skill and estimates can be inaccurate, especially for beginners.
records.practical_recommendation: Start by using broad effort descriptions; calibrate RIR over time on safe exercises.
records.misconception: RIR is an exact measurement.
records.warning: Avoid testing true failure on risky lifts just to calibrate.

records.question: What is RPE in weight training?
alternative_phrasings: How hard should a set feel?
records.short_answer: RPE is a rating of how hard a set feels; in common lifting scales, RPE 10 is maximal and RPE 8 is roughly two reps in reserve.
records.detailed_explanation: RPE helps adjust loading on days when readiness varies. It depends on honest, consistent self-assessment.
records.practical_recommendation: Use RPE 6–8 for much general work and learn the scale gradually.
records.misconception: RPE 8 means 8 repetitions.
records.warning: Do not confuse RPE with heart-rate zones.

records.question: How long should I rest between sets?
records.short_answer: Rest long enough to perform the next set with the quality your goal requires.
records.detailed_explanation: Hard compound lifts often need around 2–3 minutes or more; lighter isolation work may need less. Short rests are not automatically superior.
records.practical_recommendation: If reps or technique collapse because rest is too short, rest longer.
records.misconception: Short rest always burns more fat or builds more muscle.
records.warning: If dizzy, faint or unusually breathless, stop and assess rather than forcing the next set.

records.question: What is hypertrophy?
records.short_answer: Hypertrophy is an increase in muscle size, largely through enlargement of muscle fibres.
records.detailed_explanation: Resistance training provides a stimulus; recovery and nutrition support adaptation. Growth depends on repeated training over time.
records.practical_recommendation: Train muscles consistently with sufficient challenging work, progressive progression and adequate nutrition.
records.misconception: A pump or soreness proves growth happened.
records.warning: Avoid unrealistic transformation promises.

records.question: How many sets per muscle per week?
records.short_answer: Start with a recoverable amount and adjust; more weekly sets can help up to a point, with diminishing returns.
records.detailed_explanation: The 2026 ACSM overview identifies higher weekly volumes (≥10 sets/week) as associated with greater hypertrophy in its synthesis, but individual response and indirect work matter.
records.practical_recommendation: Track direct and indirect work; begin conservatively and add only if progress and recovery support it.
records.misconception: Everyone needs 20 sets per muscle.
records.warning: Persistent performance decline or joint pain warrants adjustment.

records.question: What workout split should I use?
records.short_answer: Choose a split that matches available days, experience, goal and preference.
records.detailed_explanation: Full-body works well for fewer days; upper/lower suits four days; PPL can suit higher-frequency routines when recovery and attendance are reliable.
records.practical_recommendation: Tell the plan generator your available days and session length; choose the simplest split that covers the goal.
records.misconception: One split is scientifically best for everyone.
records.warning: Do not cram missed sessions into one oversized workout.

records.question: Why am I not getting stronger?
records.short_answer: A plateau can come from programming, technique, recovery, inconsistent training, load jumps or normal slower progress.
records.detailed_explanation: Review trends rather than one workout. Strength is also skill-specific and affected by sleep, stress and bodyweight changes.
records.practical_recommendation: Check attendance and logging; review technique; use smaller load jumps; adjust volume only after checking recovery.
records.misconception: The only solution is to change the whole programme.
records.warning: Pain, sudden weakness or neurological symptoms need clinical assessment.

records.question: Can I lose belly fat with ab exercises?
alternative_phrasings: How do I lose lower belly fat?
records.short_answer: Ab exercises strengthen abdominal muscles, but they do not reliably burn fat only from the belly.
records.detailed_explanation: Fat distribution and loss are influenced by overall energy balance, genetics and individual physiology.
records.practical_recommendation: Use sustainable nutrition habits, whole-body activity and resistance training; train abs for strength if desired.
records.misconception: Crunches melt belly fat specifically.
records.warning: Avoid extreme dieting or body-shaming language.

records.question: Does soreness mean I had a good workout?
records.short_answer: No. Soreness is not a reliable measure of workout quality or muscle growth.
records.detailed_explanation: Novel exercises and eccentric work can cause soreness, but adaptation can occur without much soreness. Severe pain is not the goal.
records.practical_recommendation: Judge progress by performance, consistency, technique and recovery rather than soreness alone.
records.misconception: No soreness means no gains.
records.warning: Sharp, severe, worsening or unusual pain is different from ordinary soreness and needs caution.

records.question: How much protein do I need?
records.short_answer: For many healthy exercising adults, ISSN cites about 1.4–2.0 g/kg/day as a useful range; actual needs depend on context.
records.detailed_explanation: Total daily intake is more important than a narrow post-workout timing window. Protein foods or supplements can both contribute.
records.practical_recommendation: Estimate needs using body weight and context; prioritise affordable foods and a sustainable pattern.
records.misconception: You must drink a shake immediately after training.
records.warning: Medical conditions, pregnancy, adolescence or eating-disorder concerns require qualified advice.

records.question: Is creatine safe and what does it do?
records.short_answer: Creatine monohydrate is one of the best-supported sports supplements for improving repeated high-intensity exercise capacity and training adaptations.
records.detailed_explanation: It increases muscle creatine stores; some people notice early body-mass increase from water stored with muscle. It is not a steroid.
records.practical_recommendation: Use a reputable product; discuss use with a clinician if you have kidney disease, are pregnant, under 18 or have medical complexity.
records.misconception: Creatine is a steroid or automatically damages kidneys in healthy users.
records.warning: Do not provide personalised medical clearance or advise minors to supplement unsupervised.
records.evidence_text: Strong for healthy adults; medical populations need clinician

records.question: Should I do cardio if I want to build muscle?
records.short_answer: Yes. Cardio and resistance training can coexist; programme the dose and schedule around your priorities.
records.detailed_explanation: The interaction depends on volume, intensity, modality, timing and training status. A large endurance load can make recovery harder, but ordinary cardio does not automatically erase muscle gains.
records.practical_recommendation: Start with manageable cardio; separate demanding sessions when possible and protect key lifting sessions.
records.misconception: Any cardio destroys muscle.
records.warning: If exercise causes unusual symptoms, stop and seek advice.

records.question: What is Zone 2 cardio?
records.short_answer: Zone 2 is a commonly used label for lower-intensity aerobic training, but exact zone boundaries depend on the model and individual physiology.
records.detailed_explanation: Wrist-watch zones can be inaccurate; talk test and testing can help but are not interchangeable with lab thresholds.
records.practical_recommendation: Use a pace where conversation is possible for many practical sessions; individualise based on fitness and health.
records.misconception: Zone 2 is exactly the same heart rate for everyone.
records.warning: People with cardiac conditions or symptoms should follow clinician guidance.

records.question: How much cardio should I do for health?
records.short_answer: WHO recommends 150–300 minutes moderate activity or 75–150 minutes vigorous activity weekly, plus muscle strengthening on at least two days.
records.detailed_explanation: These are public-health guidelines; any movement is better than none and inactive people should build up gradually.
records.practical_recommendation: Accumulate activity in manageable sessions and reduce sedentary time.
records.misconception: You must do all cardio in one session.
records.warning: Medical limitations or concerning symptoms require individual advice.

records.question: What should I eat before or after training?
records.short_answer: Eat in a way that supports energy, comfort and your overall daily nutrition; a normal meal with protein and carbohydrate works for many people.
records.detailed_explanation: Exact timing is less important than consistent daily intake and tolerability. Training soon after a large meal may feel uncomfortable.
records.practical_recommendation: Choose a familiar meal or snack that sits well; include protein across the day.
records.misconception: You have a tiny 30-minute anabolic window or the workout is wasted.
records.warning: Clinical diets and medical nutrition needs belong to qualified professionals.

records.question: How do I improve my squat?
records.short_answer: Build a repeatable stance, brace, control the descent and use a depth you can reach with balance and comfort.
records.detailed_explanation: Anatomy, mobility, footwear, bar position and goal affect technique. There is no single stance that fits everyone.
records.practical_recommendation: Film a light set from side/front if safe; use a coach; progress load only while technique remains stable.
records.misconception: Knees must never travel past toes.
records.warning: Pain, instability or sudden loss of strength warrants assessment.

records.question: How do I improve my bench press?
records.short_answer: Practise the bench consistently, use a repeatable setup, choose sensible loading and build supporting upper-body strength.
records.detailed_explanation: Strength is specific; technique and volume distribution matter. Do not max out every session.
records.practical_recommendation: Use submaximal sets, log performance and add small load increments when earned.
records.misconception: Maxing out every week is the fastest route.
records.warning: Use safeties or a competent spotter; stop for shoulder/chest pain.

records.question: How do I improve my deadlift?
records.short_answer: Build a consistent start position, brace, keep the bar close and progress loads gradually.
records.detailed_explanation: Conventional and sumo are both valid; anatomy, comfort, rules and performance influence selection.
records.practical_recommendation: Practise submaximal technique sets; consider coaching if setup is uncertain.
records.misconception: One style is best for every body.
records.warning: Stop for sharp pain, numbness, weakness or other concerning symptoms.

records.question: Should I train when I'm sick?
records.short_answer: Do not train hard with fever, significant systemic symptoms or feeling acutely unwell; rest and return gradually when recovered.
records.detailed_explanation: Illness can affect hydration, coordination and cardiovascular strain. Mild symptoms still require judgement and infection-control consideration.
records.practical_recommendation: Prioritise rest; resume with an easier session after symptoms improve.
records.misconception: Sweating out an illness makes it leave faster.
records.warning: Chest symptoms, breathing difficulty, faintness or severe illness require medical care.

records.question: What should I do if an exercise hurts?
records.short_answer: Stop or modify the painful movement; do not force through sharp, escalating or unusual pain.
records.detailed_explanation: Not all discomfort is injury, but a chatbot cannot diagnose. Persistent or severe pain needs assessment.
records.practical_recommendation: Ask where, when and how severe; refer to clinician/physio when persistent, severe or function-limiting.
records.misconception: Pain means the exercise is working.
records.warning: Urgent care for chest pain, fainting, severe weakness, major swelling, deformity or neurological red flags.

records.question: What is a deload?
alternative_phrasings: Should I take a week off?
records.short_answer: A deload is a planned or responsive period of reduced training stress to help manage fatigue; it is a tool, not a mandatory calendar event.
records.detailed_explanation: The exact structure varies. Some users reduce sets, load, proximity to failure or training days.
records.practical_recommendation: Consider a lighter week when fatigue and performance trends justify it; return progressively.
records.misconception: Everyone must deload every fourth week.
records.warning: Persistent unexplained fatigue or symptoms may require medical evaluation.
records.evidence_text: Coaching application; evidence protocol not universal

records.question: Can women lift weights? Will it make them bulky?
records.short_answer: Yes. Resistance training benefits women; gaining large amounts of muscle takes substantial time, training and individual factors.
records.detailed_explanation: Sex does not require a completely different exercise list. Programming should reflect goals, experience and individual context.
records.practical_recommendation: Choose training based on the user's goal, not gender stereotypes.
records.misconception: Women should only use light weights or high reps.
records.warning: Pregnancy/postpartum needs individual guidance, not blanket exclusion.
records.tone_text: Respectful, lightly playful only if user invites

records.question: How do I build muscle at home with dumbbells?
records.short_answer: You can build strength and muscle at home if exercises challenge the target muscles and progress over time.
records.detailed_explanation: Use squat, hinge, push, pull, single-leg and trunk patterns; limited loads can be offset with unilateral work and reps.
records.practical_recommendation: Build a 2–4 day routine based on equipment and time.
records.misconception: Home workouts cannot build muscle.
records.warning: Check equipment condition and clear training space.

records.question: How much water should I drink?
records.short_answer: Hydration needs vary with body size, heat, sweat rate, food and session length; there is no single litre target for everyone.
records.detailed_explanation: Long/hot sessions and heavy sweating change needs. Overdrinking can also be dangerous.
records.practical_recommendation: Drink regularly and use thirst, conditions and session demands as guides; seek tailored advice for endurance events or medical issues.
records.misconception: Everyone must drink a fixed amount every hour.
records.warning: Confusion, vomiting, severe headache or collapse during/after exercise needs urgent assessment.

records.question: How do I know if I'm overtraining?
records.short_answer: Persistent fatigue and declining performance can signal that training or life stress exceeds recovery, but a chatbot cannot diagnose overtraining syndrome.
records.detailed_explanation: Check sleep, illness, nutrition, stress and workload. Overtraining syndrome is more serious than ordinary tiredness.
records.practical_recommendation: Reduce training stress, review recovery and seek healthcare advice if symptoms persist or are severe.
records.misconception: Being exhausted every day means you're training hard enough.
records.warning: Persistent unexplained fatigue, mood changes or illness warrants professional review.

records.question: How do I make a workout plan?
records.short_answer: A good plan starts with your goal, experience, available days, session length, equipment and any limitations.
records.detailed_explanation: The same programme should not be issued to a powerlifter, bodybuilder, athlete and general-fitness beginner.
records.practical_recommendation: Collect essential inputs; generate an explainable plan; include progression and alternatives.
records.misconception: One generic routine fits everyone.
records.warning: Screen safety constraints before programming.

records.question: What is body recomposition?
alternative_phrasings: Lose fat and gain muscle at same time
records.short_answer: Body recomposition means reducing fat mass while maintaining or increasing lean mass.
records.detailed_explanation: It is more achievable for beginners, returning trainees or people with higher starting body fat, but rates vary and are not guaranteed.
records.practical_recommendation: Prioritise resistance training, adequate protein, sustainable energy intake and patience.
records.misconception: You can gain muscle and lose fat rapidly at any starting point.
records.warning: Avoid aggressive dieting, especially for minors or users with eating-disorder risk.

records.question: What is the difference between strength and hypertrophy training?
records.short_answer: Strength training prioritises force and skill in specific tasks; hypertrophy training prioritises muscle growth through sufficient challenging work.
records.detailed_explanation: They overlap: bigger muscles can support strength, and strength training can grow muscle. Programming emphasis differs.
records.practical_recommendation: Choose based on primary outcome and combine when appropriate.
records.misconception: You must choose only one forever.
records.warning: Max testing and advanced loading require experience and safeguards.

records.question: What is a 1RM?
records.short_answer: A one-repetition maximum is the heaviest load you can lift once with acceptable technique.
records.detailed_explanation: It is specific to the lift and conditions. Estimates from submaximal sets are often enough for programming.
records.practical_recommendation: Use a conservative estimated 1RM when appropriate; direct testing should be supervised and planned.
records.misconception: You need to test 1RM every week.
records.warning: Do not attempt maximal lifts without experience, safeties and sound technique.

records.question: What is the difference between HIIT and steady-state cardio?
records.short_answer: HIIT uses repeated hard efforts with recovery; steady-state cardio maintains a more consistent intensity.
records.detailed_explanation: Both can improve fitness. HIIT is time-efficient but has a higher fatigue cost; choice depends on health, preference and goal.
records.practical_recommendation: Choose a mode you can recover from and do consistently.
records.misconception: HIIT is always better for fat loss.
records.warning: Beginners and people with health conditions may need gradual progression and clinical guidance.

records.question: Can older adults build muscle and strength?
records.short_answer: Yes. Appropriately prescribed resistance training can improve strength, muscle function and independence in older adults.
records.detailed_explanation: Start from current function, medical context and confidence; progression remains important.
records.practical_recommendation: Use stable exercises, suitable support and gradual loading; include balance/function when appropriate.
records.misconception: Strength training is unsafe or pointless after a certain age.
records.warning: Refer for assessment with significant comorbidities, falls, symptoms or limitations.

records.question: Can I exercise during pregnancy?
records.short_answer: For many uncomplicated pregnancies, physical activity is safe and desirable, but an individual clinical assessment and modifications may be needed.
records.detailed_explanation: Pregnancy changes physiology and movement tolerance; complications alter recommendations.
records.practical_recommendation: Encourage discussion with obstetric provider and tailor only within their guidance.
records.misconception: All pregnant people must stop exercise.
records.warning: Stop and seek obstetric advice for bleeding, fluid leakage, chest pain, dizziness, calf swelling, painful contractions or other warning signs.

records.question: How should I return after a long break?
records.short_answer: Restart below your previous training volume and loads, then rebuild gradually as tolerance and technique return.
records.detailed_explanation: Previous strength may return, but tissues, conditioning and skill may not all be at the same level.
records.practical_recommendation: Use 2–3 manageable sessions and leave extra reps in reserve initially.
records.misconception: Pick up exactly where you left off.
records.warning: If the break followed injury, surgery or illness, follow clinician guidance.

records.question: Do supplements replace a good diet?
records.short_answer: No. Supplements cannot replace adequate food, training, sleep and recovery.
records.detailed_explanation: Evidence varies by product. Creatine monohydrate and protein powder have clearer use cases than many marketed products.
records.practical_recommendation: Start by identifying a real dietary or performance need; choose third-party-tested products where possible.
records.misconception: More supplements mean faster results.
records.warning: Avoid stimulant-heavy or unverified products; medical conditions and medications require professional advice.

records.question: How do I choose an exercise alternative?
records.short_answer: Choose a substitute that preserves the movement pattern and training goal while fitting equipment, skill and comfort.
records.detailed_explanation: A substitute need not look identical; it should provide a suitable stimulus and be safe for the user.
records.practical_recommendation: Squat unavailable: leg press or goblet squat; row unavailable: supported DB row; press unavailable: push-up variation.
records.misconception: Only exercises with the same muscle label are equivalent.
records.warning: Do not use substitutions to mask unresolved pain.
